e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Beatrix, from Latin Viatrix, a woman traveler, reshaped under the influence of beatus, blessed or happy.
A modern blend of the word name Ember with the -leigh ending, on the pattern of Kimberly and Everleigh. The more common spelling is Emberly.
A K spelling of Clover, the English word for the three-leaved meadow plant, from Old English clafre. The four-leaf clover is a familiar symbol of luck.
From the Scottish surname for someone who lived by a crag, from Gaelic creag, rock. It became a common given name in the mid-20th century.
namesakes: Craig Robinson (actor and comedian of The Office)
Craig Ferguson (former host of The Late Late Show)
Craig T. Nelson (star of Coach and voice of Mr. Incredible)

assoc.t: Craig of the Creek, Cartoon Network series

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Lazarus, from Greek Lazaros, a short form of Hebrew Eleazar, God has helped. In the Gospel of John, Jesus raises Lazarus from the dead.

e.meaning: handsome (Amharic); also Latin for to love
e.etymology: Amare is an Ethiopian name from Amharic, usually glossed as handsome, and also the Latin verb to love. It rose in the US in the 2000s with basketball star Amar'e Stoudemire.

e.meaning: flowing down, from the River Jordan
e.etymology: From a medieval English short form of Jordan, the river's name, from Hebrew yarad, to go down. It became a surname and later returned to use as a given name.
namesakes: Judd Nelson (actor in The Breakfast Club)

assoc.t: the Judds: country duo Naomi and Wynonna, and Ashley Judd

e.etymology: A spelling shared by two names: Kane, from the Irish surname Ó Catháin, descendant of Cathán, from cath, battle; and the biblical Cain, firstborn of Adam and Eve, Hebrew Qayin.

assoc.t: vampire antihero of the Legacy of Kain video games

e.note: Sounds the same as Cain, who kills his brother Abel in Genesis.

e.etymology: A modern given name on the pattern of Paisley and Ainsley. Eisley is also a surname, and Mos Eisley is the desert spaceport in Star Wars.

assoc.t: Mos Eisley, the Tatooine spaceport in Star Wars

e.etymology: The German and Scandinavian form of Charles, from a Germanic word for a free man. Charlemagne, Karl der Grosse in German, made it a royal name across Europe.
namesakes: Karl Marx (philosopher and author of The Communist Manifesto)
Karl Lagerfeld (fashion designer who led Chanel)
Karl Malone (Hall of Fame NBA forward)

assoc.t: Karl Marx, author of The Communist Manifesto
Karl the Fog, San Francisco's nickname for its fog

e.etymology: Usually an elaboration of Sara, Hebrew for princess, with the -ina ending; in the US it is also a spelling of Serena. Sarina is separately a Japanese girls' name.

e.meaning: son of all (in The Neverending Story)
e.etymology: Coined by German author Michael Ende for the boy warrior of The Neverending Story (1979), where the name is said to mean son of all. The 1984 film brought it to American parents.
namesakes: Atreyu (boy warrior of The NeverEnding Story)

assoc.t: boy warrior in The NeverEnding Story

e.etymology: The Turkish form of Arabic Zaynab, popularly read as zayn ab, her father's jewel, and also the name of a fragrant flowering tree. A daughter and a granddaughter of Muhammad were named Zaynab.
Usually a modern spelling of Kailani, from Hawaiian kai, sea, and lani, sky or heaven. Read literally in Hawaiian, ka'e lani would be the edge of the sky.

assoc.t: R&B singer Kehlani, whose name sounds the same

e.etymology: A modern spelling in the family of Alaia, Alayah and Aliyah. Alaia is Basque for joyful; Aliyah comes from Hebrew and Arabic words for rising or exalted.
An Italian surname from the given name Alessio, Greek Alexios, defender. As a girl's name it works as a clipped form of Alessia or Alessandra.

assoc.t: Alessi, Italian maker of designer housewares

e.etymology: From a Scottish surname shortened from McIntyre, Gaelic Mac an tSaoir, son of the carpenter. It became a given name in African American communities in the late 20th century.
A modern American name, either a spelling of Devon, the English county, or a coinage on the Da- prefix as in Davonte and Dashawn.
A spelling of Tiana, a modern short form of Tatiana and Christiana that is also used as an elaboration of Tia.

assoc.t: Tiana, Disney's Princess and the Frog heroine (one n)

e.etymology: The Spanish form of the Italian name Gemma, from Latin gemma, a gem or a bud.
e.note: In Spanish the G sounds like an English H (HEH-mah); English speakers may read it as JEM-uh.

e.etymology: A modern American elaboration of Xavier with the -ion ending of names like Davion and Javion. Xavier itself comes from a Basque place name meaning new house.
A spelling of Adeline in its AD-uh-lin pronunciation. Adeline is a French diminutive of Adele, from the Germanic word adal, noble.
A modern combination of Lynn and Lee, also a spelling of the English surname Linley.
From Hebrew or, light, with the possessive ending: my light. It echoes Isaiah 60, Arise, shine, for your light has come, and is given to both boys and girls in Israel.

assoc.t: spirit hero of the Ori and the Blind Forest video games

e.meaning: from Lindsey, the isle of Lincoln
e.etymology: From a Scottish surname and clan name taken from Lindsey in Lincolnshire, Old English for the isle of Lind, the old name of Lincoln. It was a man's name before it caught on for girls in the 1970s.
namesakes: Lindsay Lohan (actress of Mean Girls and The Parent Trap)
Lindsay Wagner (star of The Bionic Woman)

e.etymology: From Vergilius, a Roman clan name of Etruscan origin and unknown meaning. It honors the poet Virgil, author of the Aeneid and Dante's guide in the Divine Comedy.
namesakes: Virgil (Roman poet who wrote the Aeneid)
Virgil Abloh (fashion designer who founded Off-White)
Virgil van Dijk (Liverpool and Netherlands defender)

assoc.t: Virgil, the Roman poet of the Aeneid

e.etymology: A K spelling of Calvin, from the surname of the reformer John Calvin, a Latinized form of French Cauvin, a nickname from chauve, bald.
A variant of Lena, the pet form of Helena and Magdalena, common in the US in the 1880s. It has also been explained as a feminine form of Leonard, and it is a traditional name in Estonia.

assoc.t: Lenna, the classic test photo in image processing

e.etymology: A Latinate form of Josephine, the French feminine of Joseph, from Hebrew Yosef, he will add.
From Arabic Asiya, usually explained as one who tends or consoles. In Islamic tradition Asiya was the wife of Pharaoh who raised Moses, honored as one of the greatest of women.

e.meaning: member of the Gauts, a Germanic tribe
e.etymology: A Spanish-influenced spelling of Jocelyn, used mainly in Latino families. Jocelyn comes from Old French Joscelin, a Germanic name built on the tribal name Gaut, a Geat or Goth.
A modern American coinage joining the Bray- of Brayden and Braelyn to the -leigh ending. The more common spelling is Braylee.
